title: How Insurers Are Going End-to-End in Health Care
gist: BCG interviews with 15 senior executives at mostly European health insurers find payers moving from reimbursement into end-to-end care orchestration, with every executive citing an enhanced value proposition as the goal but only half citing claims optimization and a quarter revenue diversification. The piece supplies a six-segment value-chain map, five business-model design choices, and named archetypes (AXA, Humana/CenterWell, Sanitas Spain, Vitality, Interamerican), and argues regulatory regime across 20+ countries — not ambition — determines which strategies are available.

insights.claim: Global health insurers are repositioning from claims reimbursers into orchestrators of end-to-end care, expanding along the value chain from prevention and screening through care coordination and treatment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The insurance P&L stops being a pure underwriting story and starts absorbing provider-side economics — reprice payer multiples on services mix, not just combined ratio.
insights.quote: Health insurers are reimagining their roles.
insights.locator: Health insurers are reimagining their roles

insights.claim: A growing number of health payers are pursuing vertical depth by adding company-owned or closely aligned clinics plus other physical and digital assets, rather than contracting for them at arm's length.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Watch payer capex and M&A into clinics/pharmacies as the leading indicator of vertical integration; it shifts them from asset-light to asset-heavy.
insights.quote: A growing number of payers are achieving vertical depth
insights.locator: A growing number of payers are achieving vertical depth

insights.claim: Insurers' structural advantages for orchestrating care are trusted member relationships, rich data sets, the ability to aggregate care services, and immense purchasing power — the same four assets that make disintermediation by pure providers hard.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: This is the moat argument for payer-led integration; if it holds, integrated payers should out-earn standalone providers over time.
insights.quote: Insurers are in a unique position to orchestrate end-to-end care. They have trusted relationships with members, have rich data sets, can aggregate care services, and wield immense purchasing power.
insights.locator: Insurers are in a unique position to orchestrate

insights.claim: Success in end-to-end care is gated on four execution requirements — defining strategic goals, designing the right business model, navigating regulatory boundaries, and building a delivery ecosystem — implying most attempts will fail on one of them.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Use these four as a scorecard when underwriting any payer's vertical-integration story; a miss on regulation or business model design is where value destruction shows up.
insights.quote: insurers must clearly define their strategic goals, design the right business models, navigate regulatory boundaries, and build an ecosystem for delivering services
insights.locator: To succeed, however, insurers must clearly define

insights.claim: BCG's research base for the payer value-chain expansion thesis is interviews with 15 senior executives at leading global health insurers already expanding beyond reimbursement, with the sample skewed primarily to Europe.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sample size is small and Europe-weighted — treat the conclusions as directional for EU payers and only loosely transferable to US managed care.
insights.quote: we interviewed 15 senior executives from leading global health insurers that have begun expanding beyond reimbursement
insights.locator: To understand the forces driving this trend

insights.claim: Enhancing the value proposition through better service and integrated health offerings was cited by every single one of the 15 insurer executives interviewed, making it the universal motive for value-chain expansion.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retention/engagement, not cost, is the stated primary driver — so expect spending on member-facing services ahead of measurable margin benefit.
insights.quote: Each company we interviewed cited this goal.
insights.locator: Enhance the value proposition

insights.claim: Only about half of interviewed insurer executives are pursuing claims optimization via cost control and streamlined care delivery, and just about one-quarter are targeting revenue diversification beyond insurance.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The near-term earnings case is thinner than the narrative: fewer than half are explicitly underwriting these moves on medical-cost savings or new revenue lines.
insights.quote: Around one-quarter of executives said they are looking to unlock new revenue beyond insurance.
insights.locator: Optimize claims / Diversify revenue

themes.theme: Where to Play: Value-Chain Segments and Archetypes

insights.claim: The health care value chain available to insurers splits into six addressable segments — prevention, prediction, detection, treatment, rehabilitation and management, and claims and policy management — each a distinct build-or-buy decision.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A usable map for screening payer acquisitions: which of the six segments a deal lands in tells you whether it is a cost play, a growth play, or a retention play.
insights.locator: Deciding Where to Play

insights.claim: AXA is targeting the detection segment as an "online dermatologist," using digital skin-change assessment to substitute for in-person visits and deliver fast feedback.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete template for digital-only, low-capex value-chain entry; watch whether visit substitution actually shows up in AXA's claims cost.
insights.quote: AXA is positioning itself as an “online dermatologist” by offering digital services that support early assessment of skin changes, reducing the need for in-person visits.
insights.locator: For example, AXA is positioning itself

insights.claim: Humana is executing the "primary care orchestrator" model through its CenterWell partnership, integrating primary, home, and pharmacy care with wellness and care-management programs.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The most US-relevant comparable in the piece — CenterWell is the benchmark integrated payer-provider asset for peers trying to replicate.
insights.quote: Humana is partnering with CenterWell in the “primary care orchestrator” space
insights.locator: And Humana is partnering with CenterWell

insights.claim: Three further archetypes are already live in Europe: Sanitas Spain as a "care network scaler" combining digital platforms with owned hospitals and clinics, Vitality as a "prevention champion" running personalized wellness and engagement programs, and Interamerican as an "integrated health care system" coordinating end-to-end delivery through owned assets.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Four named archetypes (plus the online-dermatologist and orchestrator models) give a taxonomy for classifying any payer's strategy and its capital intensity.
insights.quote: Similarly, Sanitas Spain is acting as a “care network scaler.”

themes.theme: Five Design Choices Mapped to Goals

insights.claim: Before expanding, a payer must resolve five design variables: service delivery model (digital-only, brick-and-mortar, or hybrid), member steerage mechanism, access and exclusivity of services, degree of business integration, and ownership model.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: These five axes are the actual differentiators between payer strategies that look identical in press releases — use them to compare deals.
insights.locator: Design Choices Shaping How Payers Expand

insights.claim: A payer's primary strategic goal should determine its business model design, so the same vertical-integration move is correct or incorrect depending on whether the aim is value proposition, claims, or revenue.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Mismatch between stated goal and chosen ownership/integration model is a red flag for execution risk in any payer vertical-integration story.
insights.quote: Generally, the insurer’s primary strategic goals are what determine its optimal business model design.
insights.locator: Generally, the insurer's primary strategic goals

insights.claim: Payers whose goal is enhancing the value proposition should stay deliberately light — hybrid delivery, steerage via information and transparency, selective external access, businesses kept separate but coordinated, and contractual alliances rather than ownership.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that value-chain expansion must mean buying clinics; the retention motive argues for partnerships, not capital deployment.
insights.locator: To enhance their value proposition, for example

insights.claim: Claims optimization argues for the most aggressive structure — active member steerage, fully integrated businesses, and equity partnerships or majority ownership — while revenue diversification argues for brick-and-mortar assets, active patient navigation, multi-payer access, and full ownership.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Only the cost and growth motives justify balance-sheet-heavy ownership; if a payer buys hospitals while citing customer experience, the design is off-thesis.
insights.quote: actively navigating member steerage, integrating the businesses, and moving toward equity partnerships or majority ownership
insights.locator: If the goal is to optimize claims

insights.claim: BCG assessed the health regulatory environments of more than 20 countries and found they collapse into three categories that determine which payer expansion strategies are even legally available.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Regulatory regime, not management ambition, sets the ceiling on payer vertical integration — screen cross-border payer comparisons by regime first.
insights.quote: We assessed the regulatory environments in more than 20 countries globally to understand how they impact payers’ options.
insights.locator: Regulatory Systems Influence the Strategic Options

insights.claim: In regulated systems with steering options, strict limits on owning health care assets push insurers toward digital partnerships, selective provider contracting, and hybrid services delivered through alliances rather than acquisition.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: In these markets, expect payer growth to show up as partnership and digital spend, not M&A — model low capex, slower integration benefit.
insights.locator: Regulated Systems with Steering Options

insights.claim: Permissive and market-driven systems allow payers to own clinics and pharmacies and access clinical data under clear governance, making revenue diversification through commercial care delivery viable; partially liberalized systems limit them to selective ownership or joint ventures in high-margin segments.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Only permissive markets support the full ownership thesis; elsewhere the realistic upside is JV economics in high-margin niches.
insights.locator: Permissive and Market-Driven Systems

insights.claim: The distinguishing success factors of leading payer value creators are leveraging customer trust to address unmet needs, resolving fee-for-service conflicts while unlocking synergies through integrated data, and building providers' management capabilities with a long-term commitment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Resolving fee-for-service conflict is the crux — a payer that owns providers but keeps fee-for-service incentives captures none of the cost synergy.
insights.quote: They optimize claims by resolving fee-for-service conflicts and unlocking synergies through integrated data.
insights.locator: Our research identified several key success factors

insights.claim: Value-chain expansion should run as a three-phase sequence — Prepare (define intent, map regulatory boundaries, mobilize a cross-functional team), Conceptualize (prioritize opportunities, make design choices, build the business case against capital requirements), and Implement (launch, track KPIs, then scale what works).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Phased sequencing means the payer capex cycle here is multi-year — near-term earnings drag before any measurable claims benefit.
insights.quote: Define the strategic intent and ambition, whether it be enhancing the value proposition, optimizing claims, or diversifying revenues.
insights.locator: Prepare / Conceptualize / Implement

insights.claim: BCG frames payer expansion as a competitive race with a finite winner set — insurers that pair the right business model for their target market with robust execution will capture the remaining growth across the health care value chain.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies dispersion, not a rising tide: expect a widening valuation gap between payers that integrate well and those that buy assets without a model.
insights.quote: For today’s health insurers, the race is on to branch out from their core businesses of reimbursing patients’ claims and become orchestrators of care.
insights.locator: For today's health insurers, the race is on
